questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding NRE accounts is correct?

options.text: Interest earned is taxable in India
Account can only be opened in foreign currency
Only resident Indians can open the account

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Funds are fully repatriable.

Key Points

  • Definition of NRE Account: A Non-Resident External (NRE) account is a bank account opened in India in the name of an NRI (Non-Resident Indian) or OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) to park their foreign earnings in Indian Rupees (INR).
  • Repatriability of Funds: One of the most significant features of an NRE account is that both the principal amount and the interest earned are fully and freely repatriable. This means the account holder can transfer the entire balance back to their foreign country of residence without any restrictions or regulatory hurdles. Hence, Statement C is correct.
  • Taxation Policy: The interest income earned on an NRE account is completely tax-free in India. According to Section 10(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, such interest is not included in the total income of the individual, provided they are a person resident outside India. Hence, Statement A is incorrect.
  • Currency of Maintenance: Although the funds are deposited in foreign currency (such as USD, GBP, or Euro), they are converted and maintained in Indian Rupees (INR) at the prevailing exchange rate. It is not a foreign currency account like an FCNR account. Hence, Statement B is incorrect.
  • Eligibility for Opening: NRE accounts can only be opened by Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs). Resident Indians are not eligible to open or hold these accounts. Hence, Statement D is incorrect.
  • Joint Holding: An NRE account can be held jointly with other NRIs or with a resident Indian relative. However, in the case of a resident relative, the account must be operated on a "former or survivor" basis. Hence, Statement E is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Governing Regulations: These accounts are strictly governed by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, and the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The rules ensure the seamless flow of foreign exchange into the Indian banking system.
  • Comparison with NRO Account: Unlike the NRE account, the NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account is used to manage income earned within India, such as rent, pension, or dividends. In an NRO account, the interest is taxable at 30% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), and there are limits on repatriation (up to USD 1 million per financial year).
  • Types of NRE Accounts: Banks in India offer NRE facilities in various formats, including Savings Accounts, Current Accounts, Recurring Deposits, and Fixed Deposits (often referred to as Term Deposits).
  • Exchange Rate Risk: Since the NRE account is maintained in Indian Rupees (INR), the account holder is exposed to currency fluctuation risk. If the Rupee depreciates against the foreign currency, the value of the funds in terms of the foreign currency might decrease at the time of repatriation.
  • FCNR (B) Accounts: For those looking to avoid exchange rate risk, the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) account is an alternative where funds are maintained in the original foreign currency and are also tax-exempt.

Important Points

  • Permissible Credits: The NRE account can be credited with fresh remittances from abroad through banking channels, transfers from other NRE/FCNR accounts, and interest or dividends on investments made from the account.
  • Nomination Facility: Account holders can nominate either a resident Indian or a non-resident. If a resident Indian is the nominee, the funds inherited upon the death of the account holder are typically credited to an NRO account and are subject to repatriation limits.
  • Impact of Change in Status: If an NRI returns to India for a permanent stay, the NRE account must be designated as a resident account or the funds must be transferred to a Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account immediately to comply with FEMA rules.

The correct answer is Person of Indian Origin.

Key Points

  • The term PIO stands for Person of Indian Origin. Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, this definition is crucial for identifying individuals who are not Indian citizens but have a lineage or historical connection to India for the purpose of financial transactions.
  • A PIO is defined as a person (other than a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, or Bhutan) who has at any time held an Indian Passport. Hence, the option Person of Indian Origin is correct.
  • It also includes any person whose father or grandfather was a citizen of India by virtue of the Constitution of India or the Citizenship Act, 1955.
  • The classification of PIO is used by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to regulate the acquisition and transfer of immovable property in India and the opening of specific types of bank accounts.
  • Under FEMA, PIOs are granted various facilities similar to Non-Resident Indians (NRIs), such as the ability to invest in Indian shares, debentures, and mutual funds on a repatriable or non-repatriable basis.

Additional Information

  • Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999:
    • FEMA replaced the older Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) in June 2000.
    • Its primary objective is to consolidate and amend the law relating to foreign exchange to facilitate external trade and payments and promote the orderly development of the foreign exchange market in India.
    • Unlike FERA, which was a prohibitive law, FEMA is a civil law that focuses on management rather than regulation through criminal penalties.
  • Merging of PIO and OCI Cards:
    • On January 9, 2015, the Government of India discontinued the PIO Card scheme and merged it with the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Card scheme.
    • Currently, most individuals previously classified as PIOs are treated as OCI cardholders under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2015.
    • OCI cardholders enjoy benefits such as a multi-purpose, multiple-entry, lifelong visa for visiting India and exemption from registration with Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) for any length of stay.
  • Distinction between NRI and PIO:
    • An NRI (Non-Resident Indian) is an Indian citizen who resides outside India for the purpose of employment, carrying on business, or for any other purpose indicating an indefinite stay.
    • A PIO is a foreign citizen (except for specific neighboring countries) who has Indian ancestry or has held an Indian passport in the past.

Important Points

  • Investment Limitations: PIOs are generally permitted to purchase residential or commercial property in India. However, they are strictly prohibited from purchasing agricultural land, plantation property, or farmhouses without prior approval from the RBI.
  • Banking Accounts: PIOs can open Non-Resident External (NRE) accounts, Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts, and Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) accounts with authorized dealers in India.
  • Repatriation: Under FEMA, PIOs can repatriate (send back to their home country) the sale proceeds of immovable property in India, subject to certain conditions and a limit of USD 1 million per financial year.
  • Taxation: Income earned by a PIO in India (such as rent, dividends, or interest) is subject to Indian Income Tax laws and the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between India and their country of residence.

questions.text: Which account is suitable for returning NRIs to maintain foreign currency funds in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is RFC Account.

Key Points

  • RFC (Resident Foreign Currency) Account is a scheme specifically designed for Returning Indians (NRIs who have returned to India for permanent settlement) to maintain their foreign currency funds. Hence, this statement is correct.
  • This account allows individuals to park their foreign earnings, such as pension, monetary gifts, or proceeds from assets held outside India, in a foreign currency without the immediate need for conversion into Indian Rupees (INR).
  • Funds from NRE (Non-Resident External) and FCNR (Foreign Currency Non-Resident) accounts can be easily transferred into an RFC account upon a person’s change of status from Non-Resident to Resident.
  • The account can be maintained in any freely convertible foreign currency, including USD (US Dollar), GBP (Great British Pound), Euro, JPY (Japanese Yen), and CAD (Canadian Dollar).
  • The RFC account is governed by the guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999.

Additional Information

  • NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) Account:
    • This account is used by NRIs to manage their Indian income, such as rent, dividends, or pension earned within India.
    • Unlike the RFC account, the NRO account is maintained in Indian Rupees (INR). Hence, this statement is incorrect.
    • Interest earned on NRO accounts is subject to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) at a rate of 30% plus applicable surcharges and cess.
  • PMJDY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana) Account:
    • Launched on 28 August 2014, it is a National Mission for Financial Inclusion to ensure access to financial services for all Indian residents.
    • It provides a Basic Savings Bank Deposit (BSBD) account with no minimum balance requirement. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
    • Key features include a RuPay Debit Card, accident insurance cover of Rs. 2 lakh, and an overdraft facility of up to Rs. 10,000 for eligible holders.
  • Demat (Dematerialized) Account:
    • A Demat account is used to hold shares and securities in electronic format, replacing physical share certificates. Hence, this statement is incorrect.
    • It is essential for trading in the Indian Stock Market and is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
  • Current Account:
    • This is a type of bank account intended for businessmen, firms, and companies that have a high volume of daily transactions.
    • These accounts generally do not earn interest and are maintained in Indian currency. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

Important Points

  • Taxation on RFC: The interest earned on an RFC account is exempt from tax as long as the individual holds the status of Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR). Once they become a full Resident, the interest becomes taxable.
  • Flexibility: Funds in an RFC account are fully repatriable, meaning they can be moved back outside India for any bonafide purpose if the account holder decides to move abroad again.
  • Joint Holding: An RFC account can be held jointly with resident relatives as defined under the Companies Act, 2013, on a "former or survivor" basis.
  • Term of Deposit: RFC accounts can be opened as Savings, Current, or Term Deposits with maturity periods typically ranging from 1 year to 3 years.

questions.text: Which of the following accounts can be jointly opened with a resident relative on a former or survivor basis?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Both NRE and NRO Accounts.

Key Points

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, allows Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) to open and maintain bank accounts in India.
  • An NRE (Non-Resident External) Account can be opened jointly with a resident relative on a ‘Former or Survivor’ basis. This means the NRI is the primary holder (Former) and the resident relative can operate the account only after the demise of the NRI. Hence, the statement regarding NRE accounts is correct.
  • An NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) Account can also be opened or held jointly with a resident relative on a ‘Former or Survivor’ basis. This helps in managing local earnings in India through a resident relative. Hence, the statement regarding NRO accounts is correct.
  • The ‘Former or Survivor’ clause ensures that during the lifetime of the NRI holder, the resident relative cannot operate the account as a joint owner but can do so only as a Power of Attorney (PoA) holder for restricted activities.
  • As per RBI guidelines, both NRE and NRO accounts are eligible for this joint holding facility with resident relatives to provide flexibility in managing funds. Hence, the combined option of both accounts is correct.

Additional Information

  • NRE (Non-Resident External) Account:
    • This account is maintained in Indian Rupees (INR).
    • It is primarily used to park foreign earnings remitted to India.
    • The principal amount and the interest earned are fully and freely repatriable outside India.
    • The interest income earned in this account is exempt from income tax in India under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
  • NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) Account:
    • This account is also maintained in Indian Rupees (INR) but is used to manage income earned within India, such as rent, dividends, or pension.
    • While funds can be deposited in foreign currency, they are stored in INR.
    • Repatriation is limited to USD 1 million per financial year (April to March) for all legitimate purposes, subject to payment of applicable taxes.
    • Interest earned on an NRO account is taxable at a base rate of 30% plus applicable surcharge and cess (TDS).
  • EEFC (Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency) Account:
    • This is a foreign currency account maintained by residents (exporters, etc.) to park their foreign exchange earnings.
    • It does not earn any interest and is not designed for NRIs to hold jointly with residents on a former or survivor basis in the same context as NRE/NRO.

Important Points

  • Definition of Relative: For the purpose of these accounts, the term ‘relative’ is defined under Section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013. It includes spouse, parents, children, step-children, siblings, etc.
  • FCNR (B) Account: The Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) account also allows joint holding with a resident relative on a ‘Former or Survivor’ basis. These accounts are maintained in foreign currencies like USD, GBP, or Euro to avoid exchange rate risks.
  • Operational Authority: Even if a resident relative is a joint holder on a ‘Former or Survivor’ basis, their right to operate the account independently only arises after the NRI holder's death. Prior to that, any operation by the resident is usually via a Power of Attorney for specific local payments.

questions.text: What is the minimum tenure generally prescribed for FCNR fixed deposits?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 1 year.

Key Points

  • The Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) account, commonly known as FCNR (B), is a fixed deposit account opened by Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) in Indian banks.
  • As per the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the minimum tenure for an FCNR (B) deposit is 1 year. Any deposit made for a period less than this duration does not qualify for interest payments.
  • The maximum tenure allowed for such deposits is generally 5 years. This ensures that the funds remain stable within the Indian banking system for a medium-term duration.
  • These accounts must be maintained in foreign currency and not in Indian Rupees (INR). Common allowable currencies include the US Dollar (USD), Pound Sterling (GBP), Euro (EUR), Japanese Yen (JPY), Australian Dollar (AUD), and Canadian Dollar (CAD).
  • One of the primary benefits of this scheme is that the interest income earned on FCNR accounts is exempt from income tax in India under current tax laws.

Additional Information

  • Repatriability: Both the principal amount and the accumulated interest in an FCNR account are fully and freely repatriable, meaning the account holder can transfer the entire sum back to their country of residence without any restrictions.
  • Exchange Rate Risk: Since the funds are held in foreign currency, the depositor is protected against currency fluctuations or the depreciation of the Indian Rupee. The risk of exchange rate conversion is borne by the bank at the time of maturity if converted to INR.
  • Eligibility: The account can be opened jointly in the names of two or more NRIs/OCIs. It can also be held jointly with a resident relative (as defined under the Companies Act, 2013) on a "former or survivor" basis.
  • Interest Rates: The interest rates for FCNR (B) deposits are regulated by the RBI and are usually linked to international benchmarks such as LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate) or SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate), depending on the currency and the tenure.
  • Comparison with NRE Accounts: Unlike Non-Resident External (NRE) accounts which are maintained in Indian Rupees, FCNR accounts mitigate forex risk because the valuation remains in the original foreign currency.

Important Points

  • Premature Withdrawal: In the event of premature withdrawal before the completion of the minimum period of 1 year, no interest is payable to the depositor. Banks may also levy a penalty for withdrawals made after 1 year but before the maturity date.
  • Loan Facility: Depositors can avail of loans against the security of FCNR (B) deposits in India or abroad, subject to specific RBI regulations and margin requirements.
  • Nomination: The facility of nomination is available for these accounts, allowing the account holder to designate a person to receive the funds in the event of their death.
  • Status Change: If the NRI returns to India for permanent settlement, the FCNR (B) account can continue until maturity at the contracted rate of interest, after which it must be converted into a Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account or a regular resident account.

questions.text: Interest earned on which of the following accounts is generally taxable in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is NRO Account.

Key Points

  • The Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) Account is a savings or fixed deposit account held in India by a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) to manage their income earned within the country. Unlike other NRI accounts, the interest earned on an NRO account is fully taxable in India. Hence, the option NRO Account is correct.
  • Taxation on this account is governed by the Income Tax Act, 1961. The interest income is subject to a Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) rate of 30%, along with applicable surcharge and education cess. This makes the effective tax rate approximately 31.2%.
  • The primary function of an NRO account is to allow NRIs to deposit Indian earnings such as rent, pensions, dividends, or professional fees. These accounts are maintained in Indian Rupees (INR).
  • The repatriability of funds from an NRO account is restricted. While the interest is freely repatriable, the principal amount has a limit of USD 1 million per financial year (April to March) for all bona fide purposes, subject to payment of applicable taxes.
  • An NRO account can be held jointly with a resident Indian on a 'former or survivor' basis, providing flexibility for family members residing in India to manage local expenses.

Additional Information

  • Non-Resident External (NRE) Account:
    • An NRE account is used by NRIs to park their foreign earnings in India. The interest earned on this account is exempt from tax in India under Section 10(4) of the Income Tax Act.
    • These accounts are fully and freely repatriable, meaning both the principal and interest can be moved back to the foreign country of residence without any numerical limit.
  • Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) Account:
    • FCNR(B) accounts allow NRIs to maintain fixed deposits in foreign currencies like USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, and AUD.
    • Similar to NRE accounts, the interest income is tax-free in India as long as the status of the individual remains NRI or RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident).
  • Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) Account:
    • This account is designed for NRIs who have returned to India for permanent settlement. It allows them to hold foreign currency assets acquired while they were non-residents.
    • The interest on an RFC account is exempt from tax only if the holder qualifies as a Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR). Once they become a full resident, the interest becomes taxable.
  • Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency (EEFC) Account:
    • An EEFC account is maintained by resident exporters to credit a percentage of their foreign exchange earnings. These are non-interest bearing accounts; therefore, the question of interest taxability usually does not arise for this specific category.

Important Points

  • Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA): NRIs residing in countries that have a DTAA with India can avail of a lower rate of TDS on their NRO account interest. This tax treaty prevents the same income from being taxed in two different countries.
  • FEMA Guidelines: All NRI accounts are regulated by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, which is overseen by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Compliance with KYC (Know Your Customer) norms is mandatory for opening and maintaining these accounts.
  • Designation Change: If a resident Indian moves abroad to become an NRI, their existing savings accounts must be designated as NRO accounts as per RBI regulations. Failing to do so can lead to penalties under FEMA.

questions.text: Who regulates NRI and PIO banking accounts in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is RBI.

Key Points

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the supreme regulatory body in India responsible for overseeing banking operations and foreign exchange management, including accounts held by NRIs (Non-Resident Indians) and PIOs (Persons of Indian Origin).
  • Under the powers conferred by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, the RBI frames the rules and regulations regarding the opening, maintaining, and operation of bank accounts by persons resident outside India.
  • The RBI issues Master Directions and circulars that dictate the permissible credits, debits, and repatriation limits for different types of non-resident accounts.
  • It ensures that Authorized Dealer (AD) banks comply with Know Your Customer (KYC) norms and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) standards specifically tailored for NRI customers to maintain financial stability.
  • The RBI also monitors the interest rate frameworks offered on foreign currency deposits to ensure they remain aligned with the country's external debt management policies and monetary policy.

Additional Information

  • NRE (Non-Resident External) Account:
    • This is a Rupee-denominated account where funds are maintained in Indian Rupees.
    • A major feature is that both the principal amount and the interest earned are fully repatriable to the foreign country of the holder.
    • The interest income earned in an NRE account is exempt from income tax in India under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
  • NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) Account:
    • This account is primarily used to manage legitimate Indian income such as rent, dividends, or pension.
    • Unlike NRE accounts, the interest income is taxable at source (TDS) at a rate of 30% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), unless modified by Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA).
    • The repatriation from NRO accounts is restricted to a numerical value of USD 1 million per financial year (April to March).
  • FCNR(B) (Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank) Account:
    • These are term deposits maintained in freely convertible foreign currencies such as USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, and AUD.
    • The primary function of this account is to protect the depositor from exchange rate fluctuations, as the funds are held in foreign currency.
    • The tenure for these deposits typically ranges from 1 year to 5 years.
  • Definition of NRI and PIO:
    • An NRI is an Indian citizen residing outside India for employment, business, or vocation for an uncertain period.
    • A PIO refers to a person (other than a citizen of Pakistan or Bangladesh) who has held an Indian passport at any time or whose parents/grandparents were citizens of India.

Important Points

  • FEMA, 1999: This Act was enacted in the year 1999 and became effective from June 1, 2000, replacing the more stringent FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act) to facilitate external trade.
  • Role of Authorized Dealers: While RBI is the regulator, the actual functions of opening accounts are carried out by Category-I Authorized Dealer banks, which are commercial banks licensed by the RBI.
  • Regulatory Oversight: The RBI uses the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) guidelines to oversee the outward remittance of funds by resident individuals, which often interacts with NRI account regulations during status changes (e.g., when a resident becomes an NRI).
  • Establishment: The Reserve Bank of India was established on April 1, 1935, and is headquartered in Mumbai, Maharashtra.

questions.text: FCNR accounts are maintained in which of the following forms?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Foreign Currency.

Key Points

  • FCNR(B) stands for Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) account, which is a specialized financial instrument intended for Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs).
  • Unlike other NRI accounts, FCNR accounts are strictly maintained in Foreign Currency. This means the funds are held in the currency in which the deposit was made, and not converted into Indian Rupees (INR).
  • The account is only permitted to be opened in the form of Term Deposits (Fixed Deposits). It cannot be opened as a savings, current, or recurring deposit account.
  • The permissible tenure for an FCNR deposit ranges from a minimum of 1 year to a maximum of 5 years.
  • Commonly accepted currencies for FCNR accounts include the US Dollar (USD), Great Britain Pound (GBP), Euro (EUR), Japanese Yen (JPY), Canadian Dollar (CAD), and Australian Dollar (AUD).

Additional Information

  • Comparison with NRE and NRO Accounts:
    • Non-Resident External (NRE) accounts and Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts are both maintained in Indian Rupees (INR), whereas FCNR is maintained in Foreign Currency.
    • In an NRE account, the exchange rate risk is borne by the depositor, while in FCNR, there is no exchange risk because the currency is not converted.
  • Taxation Benefits: According to the Income Tax Act, 1961, the interest earned on FCNR deposits is entirely tax-free in India. This makes it a highly attractive investment option for NRIs looking to park their surplus foreign earnings.
  • Repatriability: One of the primary features of the FCNR account is that both the principal amount and the accrued interest are fully and freely repatriable. This means the funds can be transferred back to the foreign country of residence at any time without any regulatory hurdles.
  • Regulatory Framework: FCNR accounts are governed by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues guidelines regarding the interest rates and the types of currencies that banks in India can accept for these deposits.

Important Points

  • Protection against Devaluation: Since FCNR accounts are held in foreign currency, depositors are protected against the potential devaluation of the Indian Rupee. If the INR weakens against the USD, the value of the FCNR deposit remains stable in USD terms.
  • Joint Ownership: An NRI is allowed to open an FCNR account jointly with other NRIs. Furthermore, they can open it with a resident Indian relative on a former or survivor basis, as defined under the Companies Act, 2013.
  • Loan Facilities: Banks in India often allow depositors to take loans against the security of their FCNR deposits. These loans can be utilized for personal or business purposes in India, subject to specific RBI regulations.
  • Nomination: Account holders have the facility to appoint a nominee, who can be either a resident or a non-resident, to receive the funds in the event of the account holder's death.

questions.text: Which type of account is primarily used by NRIs to manage income earned in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is NRO Account.

Key Points

  • NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) Account is primarily used by Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) to manage and park their income earned within India. This includes earnings such as house rent, dividends from shares, pension, or interest from other investments. Hence, this option is correct.
  • The currency of an NRO account is always Indian Rupees (INR). Even if foreign currency is deposited, it is automatically converted into rupees at the prevailing exchange rate.
  • One of the distinct features of this account is that it can be held jointly with a Resident Indian on a ‘former or survivor’ basis, facilitating easier management of local expenses.
  • Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, there are specific limits on repatriation (transferring money abroad) from an NRO account, which is currently capped at USD 1 million per financial year (from April to March).
  • The interest earned on the balance in an NRO account is taxable in India. It attracts Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) at a rate of 30% plus applicable surcharge and cess, as per the Income Tax Act, 1961.

Additional Information

  • NRE (Non-Resident External) Account:
    • This account is used by NRIs to park their earnings made outside India. The funds are held in Indian Rupees (INR). Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of managing Indian-earned income.
    • The biggest advantage is that both the principal and the interest are fully and freely repatriable (can be moved out of the country without limits).
    • The interest income earned in an NRE account is completely tax-free in India.
  • FCNR (Foreign Currency Non-Resident) Account:
    • This is a fixed deposit account that allows NRIs to maintain funds in foreign currencies like USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, and AUD. Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is not for local income management.
    • Since the funds are held in foreign currency, the depositor is protected against exchange rate fluctuations.
    • Like NRE accounts, the interest income is tax-exempt in India and the funds are fully repatriable.
  • EEFC (Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency) Account:
    • This account is maintained by resident Indians who are exchange earners (like exporters) to keep their foreign currency earnings. Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is not meant for NRIs managing Indian income.
    • It is a non-interest bearing current account.
  • RFC (Resident Foreign Currency) Account:
    • This account is for NRIs who have returned to India for permanent settlement. Hence, this statement is incorrect for active NRIs managing Indian-sourced income.
    • It allows them to keep their foreign assets and foreign currency earned while they were non-residents.

Important Points

  • Reserve Bank of India (RBI): All these accounts are regulated under the guidelines issued by the RBI and the provisions of FEMA.
  • DTAA (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement): NRIs residing in countries that have a DTAA with India can avail of lower tax rates on the interest earned in their NRO accounts by submitting required documents like the Tax Residency Certificate (TRC).
  • Tenure: While NRO and NRE accounts can be savings, current, or fixed deposits, FCNR is strictly a term deposit (fixed deposit) for a period ranging from 1 to 5 years.
  • Conversion: If an Indian resident moves abroad with the intention of staying for an indefinite period, their existing resident bank accounts must be converted into NRO accounts as per banking regulations.

questions.text: Which of the following accounts allows Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) to repatriate both principal and interest freely outside India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is NRE Account.

Key Points

  • The NRE Account (Non-Resident External) is a savings, current, or fixed deposit account opened in India by a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) to park their foreign earnings in Indian Rupees (INR).
  • A primary feature of the NRE Account is that it is fully and freely repatriable, meaning both the principal amount deposited and the interest earned can be moved back to the foreign country without any restrictions or prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Hence, option B is correct.
  • The NRO Account (Non-Resident Ordinary) is used to manage income earned within India, such as rent, dividends, or pension. While interest is repatriable, the principal amount has a repatriation limit of USD 1 million per financial year. Hence, option A is incorrect.
  • The Resident Savings Account is intended only for individuals residing in India. Once a person's status changes to NRI, they are legally required under FEMA to convert these into NRO accounts. Hence, option C is incorrect.
  • The FCNR Account (Foreign Currency Non-Resident) is a fixed deposit account maintained in foreign currencies like USD, GBP, or EUR. While it allows full repatriation of both principal and interest, it is not a standard savings account for daily transactions, and the option provided in the question specifically limited it to interest. Hence, option D is incorrect.
  • The RFC Account (Resident Foreign Currency) is designed for returning NRIs who wish to maintain their foreign earnings in foreign currency after becoming residents of India again. Hence, option E is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Taxation Benefits: One of the most significant advantages of the NRE Account is that the interest income is 100% tax-free in India under Section 10(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In contrast, NRO account interest is subject to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) at a rate of 30% plus applicable surcharges.
  • Currency Conversion: Funds in an NRE account are maintained in INR. When an NRI deposits foreign currency, it is converted at the prevailing exchange rate. This exposes the account holder to exchange rate risk if the Rupee depreciates against the foreign currency at the time of repatriation.
  • FCNR Features: Unlike NRE accounts, FCNR (B) accounts are maintained in foreign currency, which eliminates exchange rate fluctuations. These are strictly term deposits with a maturity period ranging from 1 year to 5 years.
  • NRO Limitations: The NRO account is essential for NRIs who have financial liabilities or income sources in India. However, the repatriation of funds from an NRO account requires a certificate from a Chartered Accountant (Form 15CB) and an online declaration (Form 15CA) to ensure taxes are paid.

Important Points

  • Joint Accounts: An NRI can open an NRE account jointly with another NRI. They can also open it with a resident Indian relative (as defined in the Companies Act, 2013) on a "Former or Survivor" basis.
  • FEMA Guidelines: All NRI accounts are governed by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999. It is mandatory for individuals to update their residential status with the bank within a reasonable timeframe (usually 30 days) after moving abroad to avoid penalties.
  • Nomination Facility: NRIs are allowed to nominate either a resident or a non-resident as a nominee for these accounts. In the event of the account holder's death, the resident nominee can inherit the funds in Indian Rupees, while a non-resident nominee can repatriate the funds after RBI clearance.
  • Permissible Credits: NRE accounts can only be credited with inward remittances from abroad, transfers from other NRE or FCNR accounts, or interest earned on the account itself. Local funds earned in India cannot be deposited into an NRE account.
